promptText: In a hierarchical (manager/worker) multi-agent topology with one manager and N workers, roughly how many communication edges exist, compared to a fully peer-to-peer topology where every agent can talk to every other agent?
options: N edges vs up to N(N-1) edges in peer-to-peer
N(N-1) edges vs N edges in peer-to-peer
Both topologies require exactly the same number of edges
N^2 edges in hierarchical vs N edges in peer-to-peer
explanation: A hierarchy only needs the manager to talk to each worker (N edges), while a full peer topology can need up to N(N-1) edges — this is why hierarchical designs bound coordination cost and dominate production systems.

promptText: Which of the following is NOT one of the three coordination topologies the chapter identifies as covering almost every real multi-agent design?
options: Hierarchical (manager/worker)
Pipeline (sequential handoff)
Peer/debate (decentralized)
Round-robin load balancing
explanation: The chapter names hierarchical, pipeline, and peer/debate as the three dominant topologies (or combinations of them); round-robin load balancing is a networking concept, not a multi-agent coordination topology.

promptText: What is the key difference between a "blackboard" and "message passing" as shared-state patterns for multi-agent coordination?
options: A blackboard is a shared, structured workspace every agent can read and write; message passing sends discrete, addressed payloads between specific agents
Message passing requires a relational database while a blackboard only works with an in-memory cache
A blackboard can only be used by exactly two agents; message passing scales to any number
They are two different names for the exact same underlying mechanism
explanation: Blackboards suit many agents needing visibility into an evolving shared artifact; message passing suits a clear, directed flow of control and data between specific agents. Most real systems combine both.

promptText: Why does a single mega-prompt asking one agent to simultaneously be a creative brainstormer, a skeptical fact-checker, and a terse formatter tend to underperform three separate role-scoped agents?
options: A single prompt always exceeds the model's maximum context window
The model has to hold conflicting stances at once within one generation, degrading behavior on all axes rather than specializing in any one
Multi-agent systems are always cheaper in total tokens than a single agent
Single agents are structurally incapable of using tools
explanation: This is the 'role/persona pressure' from the chapter's problem statement: models, like humans asked to be three personalities in one sentence, do this poorly, whereas separate prompts each tuned for one stance perform better on each dimension.

promptText: The Contract Net Protocol, a concept from 1980s classical multi-agent systems research, describes which mechanism?
options: A manager agent broadcasts a task announcement and candidate contractor agents bid on it, with the manager awarding the task to the best bid
A voting mechanism requiring unanimous agreement among all agents before any action executes
A cryptographic handshake protocol for authenticating agents to each other
A strict rule that agents may never communicate except through a database
explanation: Modern LLM orchestrators that dispatch a subtask to whichever specialist agent seems best suited are a direct, if informal, descendant of the Contract Net Protocol's manager-broadcasts/contractors-bid pattern.

promptText: What is "groupthink" as a failure mode in multi-agent systems?
options: Agents converge on the same answer because each one independently verified it against evidence
Agents converge on a shared (possibly wrong) answer mainly because each one defers upon seeing the others already agree, not because it was independently checked
A technique for running multiple agents concurrently instead of sequentially
Another name for the hierarchical manager/worker topology
explanation: Groupthink means agents manufacture false confidence: five agents agreeing looks like consensus but may just be five correlated copies making the same mistake, since adding more agents on the same base model doesn't add real independent perspectives.

promptText: A 4-stage sequential pipeline has each stage independently correct 90% of the time, with no verification step between stages. What is the approximate end-to-end success probability, and what does this imply about adding more unverified stages?
options: About 90%, because per-stage reliability doesn't compound across a pipeline
About 66% (0.9^4), and adding further unverified stages continues to degrade end-to-end reliability multiplicatively
About 99%, because independent stages average their errors out
About 36%, and this only becomes true after at least five stages
explanation: P(pipeline succeeds) ≈ p1×p2×p3×p4 = 0.9^4 ≈ 0.6561, roughly 66% rather than 90% — errors compound multiplicatively, which is why a verification/Critic stage is necessary to break the pure multiplicative chain.

promptText: Why do most production multi-agent systems default to a hierarchical topology instead of letting every agent talk to every other agent directly?
options: Peer-to-peer coordination is not technically supported by any LLM provider
Hierarchical topologies bound coordination cost (N edges vs up to N(N-1)) and give a single component clear authority over deciding the task is complete
Hierarchical topologies always execute faster because every worker runs concurrently
Peer-to-peer topologies require strictly more expensive underlying models
explanation: This restates the classical MAS lesson from the 1980s: centralizing coordination bounds complexity and avoids ambiguity over who has final authority, which is why hierarchy is the production default despite being no faster inherently.

promptText: Why should handoffs between agents in a pipeline use structured, schema-validated data (e.g., a Java record) rather than free-form prose?
options: Free-form prose is always more token-efficient than structured data
Structured output eliminates the need for an orchestrator entirely
It gives the downstream agent an unambiguous contract, prevents silent format drift, and shrinks the prompt-injection surface area compared to an open text blob
The MCP protocol technically forbids agents from exchanging plain text
explanation: A typed claim+source pair with length/format limits is a far weaker injection vector than free text, and it prevents downstream agents from having to re-parse or reinterpret ambiguous prose.

promptText: Why is a prompt instruction like "stop revising after 2 rounds" insufficient on its own to guarantee a Critic/Researcher revision loop actually terminates?
options: Prompts are technically incapable of containing numeric values
Model compliance with any natural-language instruction is probabilistic, not guaranteed, so termination logic that must always hold belongs in deterministic orchestrator code
LLMs cannot count past two in a single context window
Revision loops can only ever be implemented as fully synchronous blocking calls
explanation: The chapter is explicit that termination guarantees must be enforced with a hard, code-level cap (a counter in the orchestrator) rather than relying on the model's probabilistic compliance with a prompt instruction.

promptText: How does a debate pattern between two separate agents differ from a single agent reflecting on and critiquing its own prior output?
options: They are functionally identical mechanisms with different names

Debate uses genuinely separate personas/agents motivated to find fault, surfacing a wider range of errors than self-reflection, which reuses the same reasoning process that produced the original mistake
Self-reflection is always strictly more expensive in tokens than a two-agent debate
Debate can never involve a synthesizer or judge agent
explanation: Self-reflection is limited because the same underlying reasoning that made the mistake is also doing the checking, potentially sharing the same blind spot; debate's independent critique is not filtered through that same reasoning.

promptText: Why does prompt injection propagate differently — and more dangerously — in a multi-agent system compared to a single agent?
options: Multi-agent systems are inherently immune to prompt injection because agents cross-check each other automatically

An injected instruction absorbed into one agent's output becomes another agent's trusted input, effectively laundering the injection across a 'trusted peer' boundary that downstream agents scrutinize less than external input
Injection can only ever occur against the very first agent in a pipeline and never spreads further
Multi-agent systems by design never process any untrusted external content
explanation: Agents often implicitly trust messages from peer agents more than raw external content, which is exactly the assumption an injected instruction can exploit as it hops from agent to agent.

promptText: Applying Byzantine-fault-tolerance thinking loosely to a 3-agent majority vote, why is a simple majority considered fragile compared to classical BFT's requirement of 3f+1 total nodes to tolerate f arbitrarily faulty ones?
options: Because LLM agents can behave arbitrarily rather than merely failing silently — e.g. one hallucinates confidently and sways a second agent — so 3 agents cannot reliably tolerate even one bad actor the way the BFT bound requires
Because majority voting mathematically requires an even number of participating agents
Because LLM agents are structurally incapable of producing a vote at all
Because Byzantine fault tolerance is a concept that only applies to blockchain consensus, not to software agents
explanation: A naive majority vote among 3 agents is fragile because a confidently wrong agent can sway a second one that sees its confidence — production systems instead favor a larger, genuinely uncorrelated quorum or supplement voting with an evidence check.

promptText: A team wants to know whether their 3-agent debate architecture provides genuine value beyond a much simpler alternative. What is the correct baseline comparison, and why?
options: Compare only against the cheapest available model's single call, since cost is the only relevant axis

Compare against self-consistency sampling (same model, same prompt, N independent samples, majority vote) at an equivalent token budget — if debate doesn't beat this simpler technique, the extra architectural complexity isn't earning its cost
No baseline comparison is needed as long as the debate's outputs look plausible to a human reviewer
Compare only against unaided human performance, since that is the only meaningful accuracy ceiling
explanation: Many 'multi-agent' wins in the wild are actually just self-consistency sampling in a fancier wrapper — the chapter is explicit that this specific baseline comparison should be run before committing to the more expensive architecture.

promptText: A staff engineer must evaluate whether splitting a currently-working single-agent customer support assistant into six specialized agents is justified. Which approach best reflects the chapter's guidance?
options: Approve the split immediately, since more specialized agents always improve output quality
Reject the split outright, since single-agent architectures are always preferable to multi-agent ones

Identify the single agent's specific measured failure modes first, confirm each proposed split genuinely targets one of them, weigh the compounding-error/latency/cost cost against the gain, and merge any two proposed roles whose personas or toolsets don't actually conflict
Decompose the agent into however many roles the most popular multi-agent framework's example code demonstrates
explanation: The chapter insists decomposition start from evidence of specific measured failures, not architecture aesthetics, and that the final design require a clear owner for 'is this response done and correct,' validated against a baseline before shipping.
